1:
The title is not what our version makes it. Clarke says the Hebrew reads not a psalm of praise but a psalm for the confession-offering, which the Chaldee renders praise for the sacrifice of confession, and the Vulgate, Septuagint and Ethiopic follow that sense. He reports the Syriac heading too: without a name, concerning Joshua the son of Nun when he had ended the war, though under the new covenant it relates to the conversion of the Gentiles. He thinks the psalm was composed after the captivity as a form of thanksgiving. Calvin says the title may serve for a summary of the contents, and that the brevity makes long discourse unnecessary.

Whom the summons reaches is the question that follows. Calvin notes that the whole earth is invited indiscriminately, and sees in that a prophecy of the time when the Church would be gathered out of many nations. Henry allows the same, that when all nations are discipled the summons will be fully answered; but he suspects the psalm was meant in the first place for proselytes who came over to the Jews' religion out of all lands. Augustine will not have it confined at all: the psalm exhorts no single corner of the earth, no one habitation or congregation of men, but exacts jubilance on every side because it has sown blessing on every side. Does all the earth hear my voice at this moment, he asks, and yet the whole earth has heard this voice — all the earth is already jubilant in the Lord, and what is not yet jubilant will be.

On the shout itself the notes are brief and warm. Spurgeon says the original word means a glad shout, such as loyal subjects give when their king appears among them, and that a happy God should be worshipped by a happy people. The world will never be in its proper condition, he adds, until with one unanimous shout it adores the only God. Gill fills the shout with occasions: the angels made it at Christ's birth, the disciples at his entry into Jerusalem, the apostles at his ascension, and it is the shout due to a triumphant conqueror who has beaten sin, Satan, death and the grave. Ellicott adds only that the phrase may be rendered all the earth.

Why the service should be glad they explain three ways. Gill sets it against the alternative: not a slavish fear under a spirit of bondage, as the Jews had under the legal dispensation, but spiritual joy and freedom of soul under the spirit of adoption, readily and cheerfully. Clarke makes it a duty as well as a privilege, since the religion of the true God is meant to remove human misery, and the man whom the religion of Christ has not made happy does not understand it. Spurgeon puts the same by contrast, that the invitation is no funeral solemnity but a cheery exhortation, as though we were bidden to a marriage feast. Keil and Delitzsch stand further back and place the psalm at the end of a series beginning with the ninety-first, marked throughout by that mild sublimity and sunny cheerfulness we wonder at in the second part of Isaiah; this last Jubilate, they observe, is entirely the echo of the first, so that the arrangement of the whole group proves ingenious. They also look ahead to the gates, and see in the pilgrimage of all peoples to the holy mountain an Old Testament dress for the hope of their conversion, the Temple standing open to them all.
3:
One word in the third verse divides them, and Clarke will not accept the received text. He can never think it the true reading that we have not made ourselves, though it stands in the present Hebrew, the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Syriac. Was there ever a people on earth, he asks, however grossly heathenish, that did or could believe they had made themselves? Twenty-six manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi read instead his we are, one letter of the pronoun standing where the negative particle now stands; and that is the reading of the Targum, of the Complutensian Polyglot, of both Psalters printed in 1477, and the marginal reading in most Masoretic Bibles. Ellicott reports that most commentators now prefer it, since it keeps the parallelism better and has great manuscript support, and notes that the close of the verse echoes an earlier psalm.

What is to be acknowledged Clarke and Gill state differently. Clarke asks for acknowledgment in every possible way, public and private, that Jehovah — the uncreated, self-existent and eternal Being — is Elohim, the God in covenant with man to instruct, redeem and finally make him happy; and since he is our Creator he has the only right in us and over us. Gill reads the confession of Christ: own him to be God as well as man, and though a man yet no mere man, but the great God and our Saviour, so a man as to be Jehovah's fellow — Immanuel, God with us, God manifest in the flesh.

The gates are read as the church's, and the entering as public worship. Gill makes them the gates of Zion, which the Lord loves more than all the dwellings of Jacob, and the gates of Jerusalem, within which the feet of the saints stand with pleasure; and so the gates into his house and the public ordinances of it, to be entered with thankfulness for mercies temporal and spiritual. Clarke keeps the emphasis on the privilege: worship God publicly, and be thankful when you come to the house of prayer that you have such a liberty at all. He notes again that the word rendered thanksgiving is properly the confession-offering, and glosses the blessing of the name from the liturgy — speak good of his name, since we can do no other, having nothing but good to speak of our God.

The reasons given at the close are the divine attributes themselves. Clarke argues from the nature of God: goodness, the perfect and eternal opposite of all evil, is essential to him, and mercy and compassion are only modifications of that goodness — so that since his nature is eternal, his mercy must be everlasting. Truth likewise belongs essentially to an infinitely intelligent and perfect nature, and therefore endures from generation to generation, whatever he has promised being fulfilled as long as sun and moon shall last. Gill takes the goodness both providentially and in grace: he is the good Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep, and the good Samaritan who pours in the wine and oil of his love upon wounds made by sin, who went about doing good to the bodies and souls of men and continues to do good still. Clarke closes by printing the psalm in the oldest vernacular versions he has met with, the Anglo-Saxon and the Anglo-Scottish, with a literal interlineary translation of the former.
